title: Six shaders, one pixel at a time

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Picture a tiny program that runs millions of times a second, once for every pixel on your screen, and has no idea what its neighbours are doing. That's a shader. In early 2024, Antoine published six of them on Shadertoy, and in this post he walks through each one, line by line.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Start with the basics. How does a Shadertoy shader actually run?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It's one function. The GPU calls it for every pixel, every frame. It gets three things: the pixel's position, the time, and the mouse. It returns a colour. Everything you see is built from just those inputs.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So how do you get something that looks like marble or smoke out of that?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the first shader, Domain Wrapping. It starts with noise: a grid of random values, smoothly blended. Then it stacks five layers of it, each one twice as fine and half as strong, so big shapes carry small detail. The trick is to bend the coordinates with more noise before sampling. Noise of noise of noise. Each level folds the pattern further, and you get those swirling, marbled shapes.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And the colours follow the folds?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly. The final value picks between teal and khaki, and the in-between values tint it toward navy or pale cyan. So the colour traces the shape of the warp.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What's the most useful trick of the six?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Grid Line, the shortest one. It draws a grid whose lines stay exactly one pixel wide, however far you zoom. It measures how much a value changes from one pixel to the next, and uses that to convert distances into pixels. As a bonus, the one-pixel edge acts as cheap anti-aliasing.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sun Ray Clockwise. It works in polar coordinates, an angle and a distance from the centre. The angle is in degrees and feeds straight into a cosine, which turns one full circle into more than a hundred thin rays. A rotation of seventy-two degrees per second spins them clockwise, and a ring term makes them pulse in and out.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Sea and Stars. It's a collage of three well-known shaders, each credited: an ocean, a star field and clouds, plus floating spheres Antoine added. And the last one, Warping Mouse, builds on Inigo Quilez's warping work, with two levels of warp, light computed from the pattern as if it were a height map, and the mouse gently steering it.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A handful of simple ideas, noise, layering and coordinate tricks, go a very long way. The full write-up has every shader embedded, paused until you press play, with the code explained next to it.
